title: COLD OPEN — hook in the first 10 seconds
text:
This reel took me eleven minutes to make, it cost me nothing, and it's the exact three-part formula behind almost every viral reel on your feed right now. A scroll-stopping hook, punchy captions that move, and one editing trick at the end that most people never use — and the whole thing is just Canva plus CapCut, both on the free plan.

By the end of this video you'll have your own reel, built from scratch, exported the right way — and I'll show you the one export mistake that quietly kills your reach on Instagram, so stick around for that. Let's get into Canva.

title: 1.1 Set up the Reel canvas
text:
First thing: the canvas. In Canva, click Create a design, top right, and search for Instagram Reel. You want the video one — ten-eighty by nineteen-twenty, portrait. Don't grab a Story template or a Post and try to stretch it later, because your text will sit in the wrong safe zones and Instagram will crop right over it.

Before you touch anything else, look at the edges of the canvas. The top fifteen percent and the bottom twenty percent are danger zones — that's where Instagram lays its own interface, your caption, the audio tag, the share buttons. Anything important lives in the middle of the frame. Keep that in your head the whole way through.

title: 1.2 Build the hook slide
text:
Slide one is your hook, and it has one job: stop the thumb. You've got well under a second, so we're doing big text, high contrast, no clutter. Click Text, add a heading, and type your hook. I'm using "3 Canva tricks nobody shows you" — but the formula is: a number, a promise, and a hint of a secret. Steal that.

If you're staring at a blank heading wondering what to write, here are the three hook formulas that carry most viral reels. One: the number promise — "three Canva tricks nobody shows you". Two: the call-out — "if you sell on Etsy, stop making this mistake". You name your exact viewer and they physically cannot scroll past. Three: the forbidden one — "I wasn't going to share this". Curiosity does the rest. Write yours with one of those three and you're ahead of ninety percent of the feed before you've touched a single animation.

Now make it impossible to ignore. Font matters more than you think — go bold, go heavy. I'm using Archivo Black. Bump the size until it nearly touches the edges, then set your two colours: one for the background, one for the text, and make them fight each other. Dark background, electric text. If your brand colours are soft pastels, this is the one place you betray them.

One more layer: select the text, hit Effects, and add a Background — that little colour block behind the words. It keeps your hook readable even when the video behind it gets busy. That one click is doing more work than any transition you'll add later.

title: 1.3 Build slides two to four — the value
text:
Now duplicate that slide three times — the little duplicate icon, right here. Same background, same fonts, same positions. That consistency is what makes it feel designed instead of thrown together, and it means the text lands in the same spot every slide, which matters when we animate.

Slides two, three and four are your actual content — one idea per slide, one line of setup and one line of payoff. Nobody reads a paragraph in a reel. If a slide needs more than two short lines, it's two slides.

Let's make it feel alive. Photos or graphics: click Elements, and if you're dropping a product shot or a face in, use Edit photo and Background remover — yes, that's now on the free tier — so it sits on your colour instead of inside a white box.

title: 1.4 Animate and export
text:
Animation time, and here's the rule: one animation style for the whole reel. Select the page, click Animate, and look at these — for reels you want the aggressive ones. Pop, Tumble, Breathe. I'm using Pop. Click it once and it applies to the page. Do the same on every slide. Skip the gentle fades — gentle reads as slow, and slow gets scrolled.

Now timing. Each slide's got a duration on it — click the little clock. Hook slide: one and a half seconds, no longer. Content slides: two to two-and-a-half seconds each. That feels brutally fast while you're editing and exactly right when you're scrolling.

One last page before we export: duplicate your hook slide one more time and tweak it into a cover. This page never plays in the reel — it's the frame people see on your profile grid. Same hook text, but shrink it a touch and pull it dead centre, because the grid crops reels to a square. Thirty seconds now saves your profile from looking like a row of decapitated sentences.

Export. Share, top right — Download — and here's the bit people miss: file type MP4 Video, not PNG, or you lose every animation you just set. Quality ten-eighty. Download it.

Canva's done its job: it's given us a clean, branded animation. But a Canva export on its own still feels like a slideshow. CapCut is where it starts feeling like a reel.

title: 2.1 Import and lay out the timeline
text: Open CapCut, new project, and drag your Canva MP4 straight into the timeline. First job — check the frame. Ratio button says nine-sixteen, and because we designed at Reel size it should drop in perfectly, no black bars, no cropping.

title: 2.2 The music decision — this is the pro tip
text:
Now music, and this is the part that separates people who edit reels from people who post slideshows. We're going to edit to a beat. Grab the sound you want — CapCut's library is fine for editing — but remember what I said about export at the end, because we are not keeping this audio. It's scaffolding.

Right-click the track and hit beat detection — CapCut marks the beats as little dots on the audio. Now split your Canva clip so every slide change lands on a beat. Select the clip, playhead on the beat, split. When the visual hits the beat, the reel feels expensive. It's a five-minute job and it's the single biggest upgrade you can make.

title: 2.3 Auto captions with a brand style
text:
If there's any voiceover or talking in your reel, captions are not optional — most people watch with the sound off. Text, Auto captions, generate. CapCut transcribes the whole thing in about ten seconds.

Then style them once and it applies everywhere: pick a caption preset, but change the colours to yours — I'm matching the yellow from the Canva design so the whole reel feels like one thing. Bump the size, drag them to the lower third — inside that safe zone we talked about — and turn on the word-by-word animation so they pop as they're spoken.

Before you move on, actually read them. Auto captions are about ninety-five percent right, and the five percent it misses is always the word that matters — your brand name, the product, the price. Click any caption on the timeline and fix the text right there. A typo in a caption reads as careless, and careless doesn't get shared.

title: 2.4 Movement: keyframe punch-ins and one transition
text:
Even with Pop animations, static slides need camera energy. Here's the thirty-second version of a punch-in: playhead at the start of a slide, select the clip, open the scale keyframe, click the diamond. Jump to the end of the slide, scale it up to about a hundred and eight percent. That's it — a slow push-in on every slide. Subtle, constant motion.

Transitions: one. Pick one — I use a fast glitch or a whip — and put it only on the beat drop, the moment your hook slide smashes into the content. A reel with five different transitions looks like a wedding video from 2011. One transition, used once, looks intentional.

title: 2.5 The loop ending
text: Last trick before export, and this is the one almost nobody uses: make it loop. Take your last slide, and make its final frame visually identical to your first frame — same background, same layout. When the reel restarts, there's no seam. People watch it twice without noticing, your average watch time doubles, and watch time is the metric Instagram actually ranks on.

title: 2.6 Export — and the reach-killing mistake
text:
Export settings: ten-eighty P, sixty frames a second, bitrate on high — and now the thing I promised you at the start. Before you hit export, mute the music track. Yes, delete it or mute it. Here's why: if you bake a song into your file, Instagram hears it as just... your audio. But trending audio only helps your reach if it's added inside Instagram — that's how the algorithm files your reel under that sound. So: export silent — or voiceover only — then add the trending version of the track in the Instagram app when you post. You get the beat-synced edit AND the algorithm credit. That's the whole trick.

And when you do post it: the reel we just built, plus the trending audio at low volume under your voiceover, a cover frame that's readable as a thumbnail, and your hook line repeated as the first line of the caption.

title: THE 10-SECOND CHECKLIST (target ~40s)
text: Quick checklist before this thing goes anywhere near your profile — run every reel through these five. One: does something move in the first second? Two: does it make sense on mute? Three: is every word inside the safe zone? Four: does the ending loop back to the start? Five: is the music added in Instagram, not baked into the file? Five yeses and you post it. Any no, and you now know exactly which two minutes of this video to rewatch.

title: OUTRO (target ~20s)
text: So that's the full system: Canva for a branded, animated base — hook, value, loop. CapCut for the beat sync, the captions, the punch-ins, and the silent export that keeps the algorithm on your side. Total cost: nothing. Total time: about fifteen minutes once you've done it twice. If you want the Canva side to go deeper — labels, avatars, full designs — the playlist on screen has you covered. Subscribe if this saved you some guesswork, and I'll see you in the next one.
